# 2 Maccabees Chapter 12 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 12 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_012_page_001.jpg

---

**12:1** When these agreements had been reached, Lysias went back to the king, and the Jews attended to their farming.

**12:2** But certain of the governors in the various localities, namely Timothy and Apollonius the son of Gennaeus, as well as Hieronymus and Demophon, and besides these Nicanor the governor of Cyprus, would not allow them to live quietly and in peace.

**12:3** And the people of Joppa committed the following impious act: they invited the Jews who lived among them to embark with their wives and children on boats which they had provided, as though without any ill will toward them,

**12:4** and when the Jews, relying on the common vote of the city, consented, they took them out to sea and drowned them, no fewer than two hundred.

**12:5** When Judas learned what had been done to his countrymen, he gave orders to his men

**12:6** and called on God, the just judge, and went against the murderers of his kinsmen. He set fire to the harbor by night and burned the boats, and massacred those who had fled there.

**12:7** Then, because the town was closed to him, he withdrew, intending to come again to root out the whole community of Joppa.

**12:8** But learning that the people in Jamnia were minded to do the same thing to the Jews who lived among them,

**12:9** he attacked the Jamnites also by night and set fire to the harbor and the fleet, so that the glow of the light was seen in Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia away.

**12:10** When they had gone from there a distance of nine stadia in their advance against Timothy, no fewer than five thousand Arabs, along with five hundred horsemen, attacked him.

**12:11** After a fierce battle in which God helped them, the nomads were defeated, and the Arabs who had been overcome begged Judas for the right to make agreements with him, promising to give him livestock and to aid him in other matters as well.

**12:12** Judas, thinking that they would indeed be useful in many ways, agreed to make peace with them; and after the pledges had been given, they withdrew to their tents.

**12:13** He also attacked a certain city that was strongly fortified with walls and inhabited by various nationalities, whose name was Caspin.

**12:14** And those within, relying on the strength of the walls and on their supply of provisions, behaved insolently toward Judas and his men, and also railed at them, adding to the exchange of words things that were not lawful to say.

**12:15** But Maccabeus, calling on the great Sovereign of the world, who without battering rams or siege engines of war threw down Jericho in the days of Joshua, rushed wildly against the wall;

**12:16** and having taken the city by the will of God, he made unspeakable slaughters, so that the adjacent lake, two stadia wide, appeared to be running over with blood.

**12:17** From there they went seven hundred and fifty stadia and came to Charax, to the Jews who are called Tubiani.

**12:18** They did not find Timothy in those parts, for he had by then left those parts without having accomplished anything, though he had left a very strong garrison behind him in a certain place.

**12:19** But Dositheus and Sosipater, who were Maccabeus's commanders, went out and destroyed those whom Timothy had left in the stronghold, more than ten thousand men.

**12:20** And Maccabeus, arranging his army in divisions, appointed them as commanders over the divisions and hastened against Timothy, who had with him a hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred cavalry.

**12:21** When Timothy learned of the approach of Judas, he sent off the women and the children and also the baggage to a place called Carnaim, for that place was hard to besiege and difficult to approach because of the narrowness of all its passes.

**12:22** But when Judas's first division appeared, the enemies were smitten with fear and dread at the manifestation of him who sees all things, and they fled, rushing headlong in every direction, so that often they were injured by their own people and were impaled on the points of their own swords.

**12:23** And Judas pressed the pursuit vigorously and put the criminals to the sword, destroying as many as thirty thousand men.

**12:24** Timothy himself fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater and their men. But with great cunning he begged them to let him go safely, since he had the parents of most of them and the brothers of some in his possession, and to each of these harm might come.

**12:25** After he had fully confirmed his pledge to restore them unharmed, they let him go for the sake of saving their kinsmen.

**12:26** And Judas marched against Carnaim and the temple of Atargatis and slaughtered twenty-five thousand persons.

**12:27** After the rout and destruction of these enemies, he marched also against Ephron, a fortified city where large numbers of various nationalities lived. And strong young men took their stand before the walls and fought vigorously; inside there were ample supplies of military engines and missiles.

**12:28** But calling on the Sovereign who with power breaks the might of the enemies, they took the city, and slaughtered twenty-five thousand of those in it.

**12:29** Moving on from there, they marched against Scythopolis, which is six hundred stadia from Jerusalem.

**12:30** But the Jews who were settled there bore witness to the goodwill that the Scythopolitans had shown them and their kind treatment of them in the times of misfortune.

**12:31** They thanked them and exhorted them to be kindly disposed toward their race in the future as well. Then they arrived in Jerusalem, since the festival of weeks was close at hand.

**12:32** After the festival called Pentecost, they marched quickly against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.

**12:33** And Gorgias came out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.

**12:34** And when they joined battle, it happened that a few of the Jews fell.

**12:35** But a certain Dositheus, one of Bacenor's men, a horseman and powerful man, was holding Gorgias and seizing his cloak was dragging him off; and when a Thracian horseman attacked him and cut off his arm at the shoulder, Gorgias escaped to Marisa.

**12:36** As Esdris and his men had been fighting for a long time and were weary, Judas called on the Lord to show himself as their ally and leader in battle.

**12:37** Then, raising a battle cry in the Hebrew tongue, and with hymns, he surprised Gorgias's men when they were not expecting it; and he put them to flight.

**12:38** And Judas, having assembled his army, came to the city of Adullam. As the seventh day was coming on, they purified themselves according to custom and kept the sabbath there.

**12:39** On the next day, as had now become necessary, Judas and his men came to take up the bodies of the fallen and to bring them back to lie with their kindred in the sepulchres of their fathers.

**12:40** But under the tunic of each of the dead they found sacred tokens of the idols of Jamnia, which the law forbids the Jews to wear. And it became clear to all that this was the reason these men had fallen.

**12:41** So they all praised the Lord the righteous judge, who makes hidden things manifest,

**12:42** and turned to prayer, beseeching that the sin that had been committed might be wholly blotted out. And the noble Judas exhorted the people to keep themselves free from sin, having before their eyes what had happened because of the sin of those who had fallen.

**12:43** He also took up a collection, man by man, to the amount of two thousand drachmas of silver, and sent it to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering, doing it very finely and nobly with an eye toward the resurrection of the dead.

**12:44** For if he were not expecting that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead.

**12:45** But if he was looking to the splendid reward laid up for those who fall asleep in godliness, the thought was holy and pious. Therefore he made atonement for the dead, so that they might be delivered from their sin.
